content: keyframe-flow Define motion. Transform anything. keyframe-flow is a platform-independent transform and animation library for web and Node.js. It gives you a mathematically rigorous, immutable transform model, an expressive animation-definition layer, and a deterministic playback engine — with rendering delegated entirely to structural adapters you can implement yourself in three lines. The core never touches browser APIs, so the same animation code runs in a browser, in Node.js, in workers, or on a server. Interoperability with native platform matrices happens through explicit conversions that preserve mathematical meaning, never raw element copies. Why keyframe-flow - Portable by construction — zero DOM/window dependencies in the core; runs in plain Node.js (§2 principle 1 of the design docs). - One coordinate convention, stated explicitly — right-handed, column vectors, intrinsic X → Y → Z Euler order in radians, column-major matrix storage. See [Core concepts & coordinate conventions](https://johnsonjo4531.github.io/keyframe-flow/docs/core-concepts/. - Definitions are not playback — an Animation is an immutable, reusable description; every attach() yields an independent Playback instance with its own time and lifecycle. - Manual sampling is first-class — drive your own render loop with animation.sample(ms) / sampleProgress(p); no scheduler required. - Composable motion — property-level composition, groups, nested timelines, full-revolution rotation tracks, and easing built in. - Adapters, not frameworks — HTML, SVG, Canvas 2D, WebGL, and WebGPU ship as adapters; any object with setTransform(matrix) is a valid render target. Install Quick start The same definition can be sampled manually with no scheduler or target at all: Documentation - Documentation site — guides and the full API reference. - Live examples (Storybook) — every feature running in the browser. Guides in this repository live under docs/: Guide Covers --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------- [Getting started](https://johnsonjo4531.github.io/keyframe-flow/docs/getting-started/ Install, first animation, mental model [Core concepts & coordinate conventions](https://johnsonjo4531.github.io/keyframe-flow/docs/core-concepts/ Handedness, column vectors, Euler order, composition order [Animation authoring](https://johnsonjo4531.github.io/keyframe-flow/docs/animation-authoring/ From/to, property-level, keyframes, generators [Easing & interpolation](https://johnsonjo4531.github.io/keyframe-flow/docs/easing-interpolation/ Named easings, custom curves, SLERP, angular tracks [Playback & lifecycle](https://johnsonjo4531.github.io/keyframe-flow/docs/playback-lifecycle/ States, rates, repetition, promises, disposal [Render adapters & custom targets](https://johnsonjo4531.github.io/keyframe-flow/docs/render-adapters/ HTML/SVG/Canvas/WebGL/WebGPU, structural targets [Contributing docs](https://johnsonjo4531.github.io/keyframe-flow/docs/contributing-docs/ The documentation pipeline itself Internal design rationale lives in design-docs/vision.md — the source of truth the guides above link to rather than duplicate. Status keyframe-flow is pre-1.0. The public API follows semantic versioning from 0.0.0; see CHANGELOG.md. License MIT © johnsonjo4531

content: Animation An immutable, reusable animation definition (§5.1). Definitions describe motion; they are not playback instances and hold no execution state (Appendix B.1). All keyframe sources — arrays, synchronous iterables, generator instances, and functions returning iterables — are consumed eagerly and exactly once when Animation.from() is called, producing a normalized timeline that every consumer shares (§5.5). Remarks Manual sampling is first-class and requires no scheduler or render target (§10); sample(ms) and sampleProgress(p) evaluate the same timeline. Composite definitions created by Animation.combine and Animation.group evaluate through property tracks and child routing instead of materialized keyframes — their keyframes array is empty and their inputs are exposed as Animation.children (§14). --- Properties Inputs of a composite animation (combine/group); [] otherwise (§14). Total duration in milliseconds (§6.2). The eagerly normalized, frozen timeline shared by all consumers (§5.5). Composite animations built by combine/group evaluate through their Animation.children instead and expose an empty timeline here. Accessors Which transform properties this animation actually changes (§14). Keyframe timelines compare every keyframe; composite animations sample their evaluation. Property tracks built on this detection power Animation.combine and parallel groups. Methods Creates an independent playback instance from this definition (§11). The instance has its own execution state and lifecycle while sharing the definition's immutable normalized timeline — definitions are not playback instances (Appendix B.1). Attachment is optional: attach() without a target still provides full time control (play, pause, seek, repetition, completion promises) for hosts that render themselves (§11). Concurrent playbacks on the same target follow replacement semantics: the most recently started playback owns the target and supersedes the previous one without additive composition (§14). Parameters - target (RenderTarget, optional) - options (PlaybackOptions, optional) Returns - Playback Example Samples the timeline at elapsed milliseconds (§10.1). Out-of-range times are clamped to the animation boundaries; sample(500) on a 2000 ms animation is equivalent to sampleProgress(0.25). Parameters - timeMs (number) Returns - Transform Example Samples the timeline at normalized progress in [0, 1] (§10.2), evaluating the same underlying timeline as Animation.sample. Out-of-range progress is clamped to the animation boundaries. Sampling never mutates the definition and requires no scheduler or render target (§10.3). Parameters - progress (number) Returns - Transform Example Static Methods Composes independent animations into one definition through property tracks (§14): at any progress point, each input is sampled by elapsed time (shorter inputs hold their final value once complete), and the result merges per transform property — an input only overrides the properties it actually animates, with later inputs winning overlaps. The combined duration is the longest input's duration. This is the convenience layer over the track model; movement, rotation, and scale authored as separate animations compose without manually authoring a combined animation (§14). Parameters - animations (readonly Animation[]) Returns - Animation Example Creates an immutable animation definition from a from/to definition (§5.2), a property-level definition (§7), or a keyframe definition with array, iterable, generator, or factory sources (§5.3–§5.5). Keyframes are normalized and validated eagerly; invalid definitions throw here rather than failing later during sampling or playback (§6.3). Parameters - definition (AnimationDefinition) Returns - Animation Example Groups animations into a single definition — full groups and nested timelines (§14, §19). Because groups are ordinary Animation values, nesting composes naturally: groups can contain groups. Remarks - "sequence" (default): children play back to back; the group's duration is the sum of child durations. - "parallel": children run simultaneously over the longest child's duration, merging animated properties with later-wins precedence — equivalent to Animation.combine. Parameters - animations (readonly Animation[]) - options (AnimationGroupOptions, optional) Returns - Animation Example

content: Matrix4 The library's portable, canonical 4×4 matrix (§3.4, §15). Conventions (§4.4): right-handed coordinates, column vectors, column-major storage, radians for angular values. Element (row r, column c) lives at index c × 4 + r, so the translation components sit at indices 12, 13, 14 — matching WebGL/GLSL and DOMMatrix's column-major array layout (§15.2). Instances are immutable; every operation returns a new matrix (§4.2). Example --- Constructors Parameters - values (ArrayLike<number>, optional) Returns Matrix4 --- Methods Applies the matrix to a point (implicit w = 1). Parameters - point (Vector3Like) Returns - Vector3 Applies the rotation/scale part to a direction vector (implicit w = 0). Parameters - vector (Vector3Like) Returns - Vector3 Reads the element at (row, column). Parameters - row (number) - column (number) Returns - number Extracts { position, rotation, scale } from this matrix when it is mathematically decomposable into ordinary TRS components (§15.1). Throws explicitly for matrices containing shear, reflection, perspective, or singular components instead of silently approximating them (§9.2). Returns - TransformComponents Element-wise comparison within epsilon. Parameters - other (Matrix4) - epsilon (number, default: 0) Returns - boolean Returns the inverse matrix. Throws when the matrix is singular, rather than producing approximate values (§9.2). Returns - Matrix4 Raw element-wise linear interpolation between two matrices — an explicit advanced escape hatch (§9.2), never the default transform interpolation. The result is generally not TRS-decomposable (interpolated rotations gain shear); decompose it only when the inputs justify it, and accept the explicit throw otherwise. See Animation's interpolation: "raw-matrix" option for animation-level use. Parameters - other (Matrix4) - t (number) Returns - Matrix4 Matrix product this × other in conventional mathematical notation with column vectors (§4.4): the composed transform applies other first, then this. Neither operand is modified. Parameters - other (Matrix4) Returns - Matrix4 Returns a column-major number-array copy. Returns - number[] Converts to a native DOMMatrix, preserving mathematical meaning: the returned matrix applies the same transform to column vectors. Throws when the environment provides no DOMMatrix constructor — callers in browser-free environments should use toFloat32Array() or toArray(). Returns - DOMMatrixWritable Returns a column-major Float32Array copy (e.g. for GPU uploads). Returns - Float32Array Static Methods Creates a matrix from 16 values in column-major order. Parameters - values (ArrayLike<number>) Returns - Matrix4 Creates a matrix from anything exposing the named DOMMatrix members m11–m44. Conversions go through named members rather than raw array copies so mathematical meaning survives storage-order differences (§15.2). CSSOM names members as m<column><row> — the transpose of conventional mathematical m<row><column> naming. DOMMatrix transforms points as x' = x·m11 + y·m21 + z·m31 + m41, so member mXY corresponds to the element at math row Y − 1, column X − 1. Reading members in name order therefore yields exactly this library's column-major element order; "re-correcting" it would silently transpose the matrix. Parameters - other (DOMMatrixLike) Returns - Matrix4 Creates a matrix from a Float32Array interpreted as column-major values. Precision may be reduced relative to the library's internal double precision; this is inherent to the source format (§15.2). Parameters - values (Float32Array) Returns - Matrix4 Composes position, rotation, and scale into the canonical matrix T × R × S (§3.3): a point is scaled first, then rotated, then translated. Parameters - position (Vector3Like) - rotation (Quaternion) - scale (Vector3Like) Returns - Matrix4 Example The identity matrix — multiplying by it changes nothing. Returns - Matrix4

description: An independent playback instance created by Animation.attach (§11). Definitions describe motion; playback instances execute it (Appendix B.1): every instance owns its execution state — time, direction, iteration, lifecycle — while sharing the definition's immutable normalized timeline. content: Playback An independent playback instance created by Animation.attach (§11). Definitions describe motion; playback instances execute it (Appendix B.1): every instance owns its execution state — time, direction, iteration, lifecycle — while sharing the definition's immutable normalized timeline. Playback without a target is fully supported for pure time control (§11). Remarks Time semantics: Playback.currentTime is elapsed animation time in milliseconds within the current iteration, always in [0, duration]. Time progression is timestamp-based via the engine's clock, never frame-count- based (§16), and playback-rate changes never introduce discontinuities because future deltas are simply scaled by the new rate. Repetition and direction (§13) are evaluated here — the animation definition and its keyframes are never duplicated. Concurrent playbacks on one target follow replacement semantics: the most recently started playback owns the target, and superseded playbacks are cancelled without additive composition (§14). Example --- Constructors Parameters - animation (Animation) - target (RenderTarget, optional) - options (PlaybackOptions, default: {}) Returns Playback --- Properties The immutable definition being played (§11). The render target receiving evaluated transforms, if any (§11). Accessors Elapsed animation time in milliseconds within the current iteration, always clamped to [0, duration] (§11.1). The authored direction mode (§13). The completion promise of the current run (§11.1). It resolves with { status: "finished" } when all iterations complete naturally, or { status: "cancelled" } on ordinary cancellation — never a rejection. Each run started by play() gets its own promise; awaiting this getter before any run settles waits for the next settlement of whatever run is current when read. The completed iterations of the current run (§13). Configured total iterations, including the initial one (§13). The playback rate multiplier (§11.1, §16). Any finite number is accepted: 2 plays twice as fast, -1 runs backwards, 0 holds time. Changing the rate never jumps animation time — only future elapsed-time deltas are scaled relative to the current timestamp (§12, §16). Whether the current iteration runs backwards, after any reverse() calls. The current lifecycle state (§12). Methods Stops playback and resolves the run's promise with { status: "cancelled" } (§12). The last rendered transform is retained — cancellation does not attempt to restore an unknown original target transform. Cancellation and natural completion are separate outcomes; a finished or already-cancelled instance ignores this call. Returns - void Permanently releases playback resources (§12): unregisters from the engine, releases target ownership, invokes the adapter's optional dispose cleanup hook (§17.1) — never destroying the underlying DOM element, canvas context, or graphics resource (Appendix B.8) — and settles any pending finished promise as cancelled so awaiting code cannot hang. Idempotent; every other operation on a disposed instance throws (§12). Returns - void Called by the PlaybackEngine with the current clock timestamp. Advances time by the elapsed wall-clock delta scaled by playbackRate and the iteration direction — timestamp-based, never frame-count-based (§16). Parameters - timeMs (number) Returns - void Stops time advancement while retaining playback state and time (§12). A later play() resumes from the retained time. No-op unless running. Returns - void Starts or resumes playback (§12). Resuming a paused instance continues at the retained time; starting from idle, finished, or cancelled begins a new run from the beginning of the timeline in the current direction (§12) with its own Playback.finished promise. Starting (or resuming) takes target ownership, superseding any other playback on the same target (§14). Returns - void Changes playback direction (§12, §13). Time is retained and continues in the new direction from wherever it currently sits. The changed direction is also the direction a restarted run uses — play() after finishing restarts "in current direction" (§12). Returns - void Sets elapsed animation time within the current iteration, in milliseconds (§12). Out-of-range times clamp to [0, duration]. Seeking immediately re-evaluates and submits the transform to the target when one is attached, without changing playback state. Parameters - timeMs (number) Returns - void Sets normalized animation progress in [0, 1] within the current iteration (§12), equivalent to seek(progress × duration). Out-of-range progress clamps to the boundaries. Parameters - progress (number) Returns - void

title: PlaybackEngine
excerpt: PlaybackEngine The centralized playback scheduler (§16). One engine drives all active playback instances: it reads the current time from its injectable , steps every registered playback, and requests…
description: The centralized playback scheduler (§16). One engine drives all active playback instances: it reads the current time from its injectable Clock , steps every registered playback, and requests the next frame from its injectable Scheduler only while at least one playback is active — so there are no unnecessary updates when nothing is playing (§16). Animation time is timestamp-based, never frame-count-based: each update advances playbacks by the elapsed clock time scaled by their playback rate. Custom clocks and schedulers integrate without modifying the core (§21). const engine = new PlaybackEngine({ clock: myClock, scheduler: myScheduler }); const playback = animation.attach(target, { engine }); playback.play(); // driven by `engine` instead of the shared default

One engine drives all active playback instances: it reads the current time from its injectable Clock, steps every registered playback, and requests the next frame from its injectable Scheduler only while at least one playback is active — so there are no unnecessary updates when nothing is playing (§16). Animation time is timestamp-based, never frame-count-based: each update advances playbacks by the elapsed clock time scaled by their playback rate. Custom clocks and schedulers integrate without modifying the core (§21). --- Constructors Parameters - options (PlaybackEngineOptions, default: {}) Returns PlaybackEngine --- Properties The time source this engine reads timestamps from. Parameters - playback (EngineTickable) Returns - void Stops scheduling entirely (pending frame cancelled, active set cleared). Used by hosts that want to shut an engine down; playbacks can re-register afterwards. Returns - void

content: Quaternion An immutable unit-friendly quaternion used as the library's internal rotation representation (§4.3). Components follow the Hamilton convention (x, y, z, w) with w as the scalar part. Multiplication follows matrix conventions for column vectors: a.multiply(b) produces the rotation that applies b first and then a, mirroring A × B in §4.4. Example --- Constructors Parameters - x (number, default: 0) - y (number, default: 0) - z (number, default: 0) - w (number, default: 1) Returns Quaternion --- Properties Scalar part. Vector part X. Vector part Y. Vector part Z. Methods Internal non-coercing product; never exposed so inputs stay immutable. Parameters - q (Quaternion) Returns - Quaternion The conjugate; for unit quaternions this is also the inverse. Returns - Quaternion Dot product of the four components (cosine between unit orientations). Parameters - other (QuaternionObject) Returns - number Component-wise comparison within epsilon (inclusive). Note q and -q describe the same orientation but do not compare equal here — use Quaternion#dot (|dot| ≈ 1) for orientation equality. Parameters - other (QuaternionObject) - epsilon (number, default: 0) Returns - boolean Euclidean norm of the four components. Returns - number Hamilton product this ⊗ other — the rotation that applies other first, then this. Returns a new quaternion. Parameters - other (QuaternionObject) Returns - Quaternion Returns a unit-length copy. Throws on zero-length quaternions. Returns - Quaternion Rotates a vector by this quaternion: v' = q · v · q*. Parameters - v (Vector3Like) Returns - Vector3 Spherical linear interpolation toward other at parameter t ∈ [0, 1]. Inputs are normalized before use and the shortest path on the 4D sphere is taken by default (§9.1). Endpoints reproduce the inputs exactly. Parameters - other (QuaternionObject) - t (number) Returns - Quaternion The [x, y, z, w] tuple form (Hamilton order). Returns - [number, number, number, number] Decomposes this rotation into Euler angles in radians, in the inverse of Quaternion.fromEuler's intrinsic X → Y → Z convention (the angles whose Rx · Ry · Rz matrix reproduces this orientation). Angles are chosen by principal-value asin/atan2, so results need not match any particular authored triple numerically — only the resulting orientation. At the gimbal-lock poses (Y at ±90°) the X and Z angles are ambiguous; this decomposition resolves them by convention with Z set to zero. Used by angular rotation tracks (§9.1) when authored angles are not available. Returns - readonly [number, number, number] Static Methods Coerces a {x, y, z, w} object into a Quaternion. Parameters - value (QuaternionObject) Returns - Quaternion Creates a quaternion for a rotation of angle radians about axis using the right-hand rule (§4.4). The axis is normalized first. Parameters - axis (Vector3Like) - angle (number) Returns - Quaternion Creates a quaternion from Euler angles in radians (§4.3). Angles are applied as intrinsic rotations in X → Y → Z order (each about the frame produced by the previous rotation), which is equivalent to the matrix product Rx · Ry · Rz acting on column vectors. Parameters - x (number) - y (number) - z (number) Returns - Quaternion The identity rotation (0, 0, 0, 1) — no rotation at all. Returns - Quaternion

title: Transform
excerpt: Transform An immutable transform with the canonical component representation (§4.3), available as the frozen property. Euler angles are accepted only as a construction interface in radians; rotations…
description: An immutable transform with the canonical component representation { position, rotation: Quaternion, scale } (§4.3), available as the frozen components property. Euler angles are accepted only as a construction interface in radians; rotations are stored internally as quaternions (§4.3). Every operation returns a new transform without modifying its source (§4.2). Composition follows §4.4 exactly: fluent operations are applied in call order as local-space operations (right-multiplication, M ← M × Op ), and parent-to-child composition uses Parent × Local . When a composed result cannot be represented as ordinary TRS components — for example rotation appended after non-uniform scale, which introduces shear — the operation throws explicitly rather than silently approximating (§4.3, §9.2). Use Matrix4 directly for such matrices.

content: WebGLRenderTarget WebGL render target adapter (§3.6, §20 M5). title: Animation Authoring
excerpt: Animation Authoring accepts several definition styles — they all produce the same immutable, normalized timeline (§5). An is a description: it holds no execution state, so one definition can back any…
content: Animation Authoring Animation.from() accepts several definition styles — they all produce the same immutable, normalized timeline (§5). An Animation is a description: it holds no execution state, so one definition can back any number of playback instances and sampling calls. From/to definitions The simplest shape gives an explicit start and end transform over a duration in milliseconds (§5.2): Durations must be finite and non-negative; duration: 0 is legal and renders the terminal value immediately (§6.2). Property-level definitions You rarely need a full transform on both ends — specify only the properties that change, and everything else is preserved from the start (or from documented identity defaults when from is omitted) (§7): Keyframe definitions Explicit keyframes use normalized timestamps in [0, 1] — they are fractions of the timeline, independent of duration (§6.1). Re-timing an animation never requires rewriting its keyframes: Validation is eager and strict (§6.3): timestamps must be finite, in [0, 1], and strictly increasing — duplicates or out-of-order entries throw at Animation.from() time rather than being silently reordered. An empty source throws; a single keyframe produces a constant animation. Generators and iterables Any synchronous iterable works as a keyframe source — arrays, Maps, generator functions, generator instances (§5.3–§5.5). The source is consumed eagerly and exactly once , when Animation.from() runs; the normalized timeline is frozen and shared thereafter: Asynchronous iterables are rejected explicitly: normalization must complete synchronously so sampling is always available and deterministic. Composition: combine and group Independent animations can be composed instead of hand-authoring one big timeline (§14). Animation.combine merges by property track : each input only overrides the properties it actually animates, later inputs win overlaps, and shorter inputs hold their final value after completing. Animation.group builds timelines: children play back to back by default (sequence), or simultaneously with the same property-merge semantics as combine (layout: "parallel"). Groups are ordinary Animation values, so they nest freely (§14, §19): What to read next - Easing & interpolation — how values move between keyframes. - Playback & lifecycle — running definitions. content: Contributing Docs Everything on the documentation site is generated or authored in this repository — no hosted CMS, no manual HTML. This page documents the pipeline. What lives where Path Role Built by ----------------------------------- ----------------------------------------- ----------------------------------- docs/*.md User-facing guides (authored) copied into the API reference build README.md Library landing page (GitHub + docs home) same typedoc.json API reference + theme configuration — site/docs/ Generated API reference & guides make build-docs examples/.storybook/ Storybook config — examples/stories/**/*.stories.tsx Live examples (authored) — site/storybook/ Built Storybook make build-storybook docs/site-index.html Combined-site landing page copied by deploy target site/ Whole staging site both targets The published site is a single GitHub Pages deployment: guides + API reference at /keyframe-flow/docs/, examples at /keyframe-flow/storybook/, and the landing page at the root. Building locally Preview the combined site after also copying the landing page: site/ is generated output — never edit files inside it directly, and never commit it. The theme emits _assets/ and _islands/ directories. Jekyll (which runs on GitHub Pages by default) strips underscore-prefixed paths, so the deploy target always stages a .nojekyll marker at the site root. Without it the deployed site renders unstyled. Docs base paths GitHub Pages hosts this project under /keyframe-flow/, and every base path must agree: - typedoc.json → cleanJsdocTheme.basePath: /keyframe-flow/docs (the API reference lives in a sub-path of the site, not its root). - Storybook build: output served from /keyframe-flow/storybook/; builder-vite emits fully relative asset URLs, so the site is portable under any mount path (no --base-path flag exists in Storybook 10). - Guide links to other sites/pages use root-absolute paths (/keyframe-flow/storybook/…) so they resolve identically from any docs sub-page. Authoring guides Guides are Markdown with flat frontmatter for sidebar placement: - group must appear in cleanJsdocTheme.docGroups (typedoc.json) to control section order; unlisted groups are appended. - order sorts within the group. - Cross-link symbols with {@link SymbolName} — the theme resolves them to real API pages at build time. Unresolved namepaths silently render as inline code, so after adding links, grep the built HTML: - Keep guides user-facing; design rationale stays in design-docs/vision.md and is referenced by section number (§5, §17, …), not duplicated. JSDoc rules for public exports Every public export needs a description, @param/@returns where it takes arguments or returns values, at least one runnable @example, and {@link} references to related symbols. The TypeDoc build runs with theme strict: true and must stay warning-free — treat any new warning from make build-docs as a broken build. Common sources: - A public signature referencing an undocumented, unexported type (export it or document it). - {@link} targets that don't exist in the export graph. - Relative Markdown links pointing at files outside the docs inputs. Storybook stories Stories live in examples/stories/ and mount a real keyframe-flow animation into a React host with working controls (duration, easing, play/pause). Add a story when a feature ships without one; naming follows the guide structure (e.g. Playback/Lifecycle). The Code panel is enabled globally (parameters.docs.codePanel: true in .storybook/preview.tsx, backed by the @storybook/addon-docs addon) so each story shows its source next to the canvas. Storybook's auto-generated snippet collapses to a minified <l …/> tag in production builds, so an enforce: "pre" Vite plugin (injectStorySourcePlugin in .storybook/main.ts) appends each story file's verbatim TSX into meta.parameters.docs.source.code. If you add a new story file, keep the const meta = …; export default meta; shape — that is what the plugin looks for. Deploy Builds docs and Storybook into site/, stages the landing page + .nojekyll, and publishes site/ to the gh-pages branch via gh-pages. The workflow is purely Makefile-driven — no CI file needed for now.

title: Core Concepts & Coordinate Conventions
excerpt: Core Concepts & Coordinate Conventions keyframe-flow's value comes from stating one coordinate convention and never breaking it. This page is the contract (§4, §15); violations are impossible rather…
content: Core Concepts & Coordinate Conventions keyframe-flow's value comes from stating one coordinate convention and never breaking it. This page is the contract (§4, §15); violations are impossible rather than merely discouraged, because every operation that could introduce ambiguity throws explicitly. One convention, stated in full Aspect Choice --------------- -------------------------------------------------- Handedness Right-handed Vectors Column vectors — matrices act as M · v Euler order Intrinsic X → Y → Z, radians only TRS composition M = T × R × S (scale applied first to the point) Matrix storage Column-major (Float64Array[16]) Angle units Radians everywhere — degrees are never accepted Because this is fixed, two transforms produced by different parts of your codebase always compose correctly, and matrices can cross the browser/Node boundary without silent reinterpretation. Right-handedness and column vectors Vectors are columns; a matrix maps them by left-multiplication: v' = M · v. The three basis images live in the first three columns of M: This layout is exactly what WebGL's gl.uniformMatrix4fv and WGSL's mat4x4<f32> consume, and it maps onto CSS/DOMMatrix without transposition. Euler angles are intrinsic X → Y → Z, in radians Degrees are rejected structurally: there is no API surface that accepts them, so a degrees/radians mix-up cannot occur silently (§4.3). Composition order — the rule that prevents 90% of bugs Transform composition follows the parent-to-child reading M_world = M_parent × M_local (§4.4). The fluent API applies operations as local-space operations in call order, i.e. each call does M ← M × Op: For operations expressed in the parent (world) frame, use the world* variants — worldTranslate, worldRotateX/Y/Z, worldRotate — which apply in the parent frame rather than the local one. Immutability everywhere Every operation returns a new value; nothing mutates in place (§4.2). Transforms are frozen, so shared definitions can be handed to any number of playbacks without defensive copies or aliasing surprises. Negative scale is rejected at construction — mirror geometry is expressed with rotation or an explicit matrix instead, keeping decompositions unambiguous. Explicit throws over silent approximations Decomposition (matrix → position/rotation/scale) only succeeds for matrices that are TRS-decomposable. Unsupported inputs throw rather than guessing: - shear - reflection (negative determinant scale) - perspective rows - singular matrices (§9.2, §15.1) The same philosophy governs interpolation: raw element-wise matrix averaging is never the default, and opting into it (Easing & interpolation) still throws when a midpoint is not decomposable. Native matrix interop Conversions to and from platform matrices preserve mathematical meaning , not raw element order (§15.2). DOMMatrix named members follow the CSSOM m<column><row> convention, which aligns with column-major storage: The core itself imports nothing browser-specific — Matrix4.fromDOMMatrix accepts any object with the named members, structurally (§2 principle 1). See also - API reference: [Transform](../transform//, [Matrix4](../matrix4//, [Quaternion](../quaternion// - Animation authoring — building on these types - Render adapters — how the conventions surface in CSS, SVG, and GPU upload paths

title: Easing & Interpolation
excerpt: Easing & Interpolation Easing controls when values arrive; interpolation controls how they move between keyframes. Both are chosen at definition time and evaluated deterministically (§8, §9). Named…
content: Easing & Interpolation Easing controls when values arrive; interpolation controls how they move between keyframes. Both are chosen at definition time and evaluated deterministically (§8, §9). Named easings Twenty-six built-ins cover the common curves — linear, the CSS keyword family (ease, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out), and sine/quad/cubic/ quart/quint/expo/circ in each of in / out / in-out: Names are validated eagerly — an unknown easing name throws at Animation.from(), not during playback. Custom easings Any (progress: number) => number function works with no registration step (§8). Inputs and outputs are normalized progress in [0, 1]; the function must return finite numbers (non-finite results throw at sampling time): Per-keyframe segment easing The animation-level easing is the default . A keyframe may carry its own easing, which then controls interpolation from that keyframe to the next (§8): Interpolation model Between two keyframes, each transform property interpolates by its own rule (§9): Property Rule -------- ----------------------------------- Position Linear component-wise Scale Linear component-wise Rotation Quaternion SLERP , shortest path Shortest-path SLERP is the right default for orientations — but it means a rotation from 0 to 2π animates nothing , because both endpoints are the same orientation. That is where angular tracks come in. Angular rotation tracks (full revolutions) Set rotationMode: "angular" to interpolate authored Euler angles component-wise instead of collapsing to orientations (§9.1). A segment from 0 to 2π now performs one full revolution — no intermediate keyframes: Angles are captured verbatim when you author rotation as an [x, y, z] tuple; quaternion-authored values are decomposed to principal angles instead. A single quaternion cannot express "how many turns", which is exactly the information angular tracks preserve. Raw matrix interpolation For advanced hosts, interpolation: "raw-matrix" switches sampling to explicit element-wise Matrix4.lerp of endpoint matrices (§9.2). It matches property-aware interpolation for translation-only motion, and throws loudly — never approximates — when a midpoint is not TRS-decomposable (interpolating between different-axis rotations produces shear): rotationMode: "angular" and interpolation: "raw-matrix" conflict (raw matrices never consult rotation tracks) — the combination throws at definition time. title: Getting Started
excerpt: Getting Started keyframe-flow lets you describe motion once and replay it anywhere — in a browser, in Node.js, or in your own render loop. This guide takes you from an empty project to a running…
content: Getting Started keyframe-flow lets you describe motion once and replay it anywhere — in a browser, in Node.js, or in your own render loop. This guide takes you from an empty project to a running animation. The internal design rationale lives in the vision document. Guides here link to its sections (like §5) rather than duplicating them. Install The package ships ES modules with bundled type definitions. There is no browser-only entry point — the same import works in Node.js. Your first animation An animation has three parts: a definition (what moves), a playback (when and how it plays), and an optional render target (where it appears). target.html(element) writes CSS matrix3d() transforms onto the element. Swap in target.svg(gElement), target.canvas(ctx2d), or your own object — see Render adapters & custom targets. Sample without playing Manual sampling is first-class: definitions can be evaluated at any time with no scheduler, no playback instance, and no render target (§10). This is the hook for hosts that already run their own frame loop. sample(ms) and sampleProgress(p) evaluate the identical timeline; inputs outside [0, duration] or [0, 1] clamp to the boundaries. The three-object model Object Role Mutable? Reusable? ------------- ---------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------ --------------------------------------------------------- Animation Describes motion (keyframes, duration, easing) No — frozen after Animation.from() Yes — attach as many playbacks as you like Playback Executes one run: time, direction, rate, state Yes — its own execution state One lifecycle; create a new instance to restart cleanly Render target Receives evaluated Matrix4 values Host-owned Yes — the latest playback owns it (replacement semantics) Keeping these separate is what makes definitions shareable across playbacks and targets swappable without touching animation code (Appendix B.1). What to read next - Core concepts & coordinate conventions — the math contract: handedness, column vectors, Euler order, composition order. - Animation authoring — from/to, property-level, keyframes, and generator sources. - Easing & interpolation — named easings, custom curves, SLERP, and full-revolution rotation tracks. - Playback & lifecycle — the full state machine, rates, repetition, and disposal. - Render adapters & custom targets — HTML, SVG, Canvas, WebGL, WebGPU, and rolling your own. Live versions of every example run in the Storybook examples.

title: Playback & Lifecycle
excerpt: Playback & Lifecycle creates an independent — a stateful execution of an immutable definition (§11). Multiple playbacks can run from the same definition simultaneously; each owns its own time,…
content: Playback & Lifecycle animation.attach() creates an independent Playback — a stateful execution of an immutable definition (§11). Multiple playbacks can run from the same definition simultaneously; each owns its own time, direction, rate, and lifecycle (Appendix B.1). Attaching The target is optional — animation.attach() with no target still gives full time control for hosts that render themselves by reading playback.currentTime and sampling the animation (§10.3). The state machine (§12) States: idle → running ⇄ paused → finished | cancelled, plus terminal disposed. Key guarantees: - currentTime is elapsed animation time within the current iteration, clamped to [0, duration] — it is not wall-clock time. - finished never rejects. It resolves with a status object; awaiting it from idle waits for the first run, and every new run exposes a fresh promise. Code that awaits can therefore never hang: disposal settles any pending wait as { status: "cancelled" }. - Disposal is resource release, not destruction. The animation definition, the render target, and any DOM/GPU objects survive untouched (Appendix B.8); adapter-level cleanup hooks run at most once. Playback rate playbackRate is settable while running and continuous — changing it never teleports currentTime, it only changes how fast time advances afterwards. Negative rates play backwards; combined with direction: "alternate" the two compose predictably (§13). Repetition and direction (§13) Repetition is handled by the engine loop, not by duplicating keyframes: - iterations: n runs n times (including the first); "infinite" never completes — finished stays pending until cancel/dispose. - direction: "reverse" plays each iteration backwards; "alternate" flips per iteration; "alternate-reverse" starts reversed. - Multiple iteration boundaries can be crossed in a single frame (long stalls, high rates) without losing sync — time is computed from timestamps, never counted per frame (§16). Target ownership: replacement, not composition (§14) Starting a playback on a target supersedes the previous owner: the older playback is cancelled (its finished resolves { status: "cancelled" }) and the newest one exclusively drives the target. There is no additive blending — if you want two motions to combine, compose the animations first with Animation.combine, then attach once. Deterministic testing with manual timing Timekeeping and scheduling are injectable interfaces kept separate (§16). In tests, drive everything by hand — no timers, no flake: The default engine is created lazily on first use with the system clock and a requestAnimationFrame-based scheduler (falling back to timers in Node), so normal usage needs no setup. See also - Render adapters — what targets receive and own. - Live lifecycle playground in the Storybook examples.

title: Render Adapters & Custom Targets
excerpt: Render Adapters & Custom Targets A render target is any object with a method (§17.1). That's the entire contract — no base class, no imports from this library required inside your renderer: Adapters…
content: Render Adapters & Custom Targets A render target is any object with a setTransform(matrix) method (§17.1). That's the entire contract — no base class, no imports from this library required inside your renderer: Adapters own rendering state only — they never touch playback time or lifecycle (§3.6), and disposing a playback never destroys the host's element, context, or GPU resources (Appendix B.8). An optional dispose() hook on the target lets adapters release whatever they allocated; it runs at most once. HTML — target.html(element) Writes CSS matrix3d() values in column-major argument order — no transposition, verified against the browser's own CSS parser: Because the adapter owns the inline transform property, any pre-existing transform is replaced on the first evaluated frame. A one-time origin can be set explicitly (§17.3): SVG — target.svg(element) Writes the SVG 1.1 transform="matrix(a, b, c, d, e, f)" attribute mapped from the matrix's column vectors. SVG is inherently 2D affine here: Z and perspective members are not expressible and are dropped by design (§17). Canvas 2D — target.canvas(context) A 4×4 matrix cannot be applied to a 2D context directly, so the adapter runs an explicit projection step rather than forwarding raw values (§17.3): the origin and X/Y basis images are projected through homogeneous perspective division with an optional camera distance, and the fitted affine is installed with setTransform — which replaces the CTM deterministically (it composes nothing). The projection is exposed as the pure function projectToCanvas2D(matrix, options) if you need it in your own draw code. WebGL — target.webgl(options) GPU adapters own only rendering state: the latest evaluated transform as a column-major Float32Array — exactly what gl.uniformMatrix4fv and GLSL mat4 consume (§15). No GL resources are created; you upload (and draw) in the hook or from your own loop: WebGPU — target.webgpu(options) Identical shape to WebGL for WGSL hosts: the same column-major layout matches mat4x4<f32> uniforms element-for-element (§15). Device, queue, and command encoder ownership stay entirely host-side — encode your draw calls in onTransform. Ownership and disposal semantics (§17.2) - The most recently started playback owns a target; starting another one supersedes the previous owner (replacement, never additive — §14). - playback.dispose() runs the adapter's optional dispose() hook but leaves host objects fully intact: elements keep their last transform and remain writable, contexts stay usable, custom target data survives. - Adapters are reusable after disposal — nothing GPU/DOM-side is destroyed by library code (Appendix B.8). See also - API reference for the RenderTarget interface and adapter factories. - Live HTML/SVG/Canvas/custom-target demos in the Storybook examples.
